item.content:encoded:
Spanish studio NUA Arquitectures has completed Casa Juià, a farmhouse in Catalonia that draws on the craftsmanship of the surrounding region.

Located in the village of Juià, at the foot of the Gavarres mountain range in Spain, the 283-square-metre home comprises three parallel wings wrapped in porches and galleries.

Casa Juià reinterprets the region's traditional farmhouse typology, known as masia, and also takes cues from neighbouring structures, local roof forms and the site's original terrain.

"The project is conceived as a contemporary interpretation of the traditional Catalan farmhouse," NUA arquitectures co-founder Arnau Tiñena told Dezeen.

Casa Juià was built for a family of five who returned to rural life after several years in a city.

The house stands opposite a traditional rural farmhouse on Mas Nadal, a road on the edge of Juià, at the transition between the village and a forest of cork, pine and oak.

"Its central idea is to inhabit the transition between the village and the forest, creating an architecture that is deeply rooted in its context while expressing a clear contemporary identity," said studio partner Ferran Tiñena.

"The house mirrors an existing farmhouse and reinterprets it in typology, moving away from romanticism and literal imitation," added Arnau.

The farmhouse's layout, materials and handcrafted construction methods were chosen to celebrate local knowledge, while also tending towards more contemporary design.

It is arranged as three parallel, two-storey wings that give the building a clear order within the rougher surrounding terrain.

"The linear structure allows the dwelling to unfold as a sequence of interconnected spaces that extend toward the landscape," said Ferran.

A staircase leads from the garden up to a double-height entrance, which opens onto the ground-floor living areas, with bedrooms above.

Read:

Madras Spaces creates rural Indian home using "only what was necessary"

On the ground floor, the interiors extend onto a covered porch, while upstairs they lead onto a gallery – opening the house to scenic views. The staggered arrangement of these porches and galleries is intended to evoke the layout and passive climate control found in the local farmhouses.

The east-west axis of the site is left open to maximise sunlight, cross-ventilation and views over the fields, while the enclosed north-south axis borders the forest and adjacent properties, and features solid, thermally efficient walls.

"The design is entirely shaped by the specific conditions of the site, reinforcing the idea of the house as a passage through the land," said Arnau.

"Equally significant is the careful framing of views, which establishes a constant dialogue with the surrounding landscape."

Casa Juià's material palette was chosen for its texture and durability. Timber, ceramic and lime mortar are used throughout the project, each locally sourced and central to the local construction industry.

"All three of the primary materials used in Casa Juià are natural, locally sourced materials with a low environmental footprint, deeply rooted in the region's construction culture," said Arnau.

Timber is used for the house's floor beams, joinery and custom-designed furniture, while ceramic forms the roof covering and protective waterproof cladding on the facades, as well as the flooring and wall finishes inside.

Lime mortar glazes the exterior facade and many of the interior walls.

"Materiality plays a fundamental role in the identity of the project," said Arnau. "It celebrates the honesty of construction rather than concealing it."

Local craftsmanship shaped the handmade finishes and custom-built elements throughout, which were designed to preserve the imperfections and character of the structure rather than smooth them away.

"Materials are not only a construction system but also an expression of local culture, craftsmanship and time," Ferran continued. "By prioritising local materials, collaborating with regional craftspeople and supporting traditional building techniques, the project reinforces local knowledge and contributes to the circular economy."

Other farmhouses recently featured on Dezeen include a Highlands house with blackened-larch extension by Loader Monteith, a 1970s timber-and-brick farmhouse by Bastiaan Jongerius Architecten and a 19th-century Somerset by Forgeworks.

The photography is by José Hevia.

item.content:encoded:
A large multi-generational home in India and a low-lying stone farmhouse in rural Scotland are among the mix of residences in this eclectic edition of Dezeen's houses of the month.

Also on the list of the five most popular houses featured on Dezeen in July are a gridded forest dwelling in the Netherlands, a rammed-earth courtyard house in New Zealand and a stepped home on the Mexican coast.

Read on to find out more about Dezeen readers' favourite houses this month:

Dulnain, Scotland, by Loader Monteith

The most popular house on Dezeen this month was Dulnain, a three-bedroom family home in the Scottish Highlands.

Designed by Loader Monteith, the project involved rebuilding a derelict farmhouse and adding a blackened-larch extension that divides the home into two wings. Approximately 90 per cent of the building's original granite blocks were repurposed for the build.

Find out more about Dulnain ›

Forest Villa MB, the Netherlands, by Tom Kneepkens

A gridded timber roof overhangs Forest Villa MB, which architect Tom Kneepkens designed to feel connected to its woodland site in the Netherlands.

The roof incorporates openings through which trees can grow, while large expanses of glazing allow plenty of views out to nature.

"Rather than imposing itself on the landscape, the architecture adapts to the natural environment, allowing the built structure and the existing vegetation to coexist," said Kneepkens.

Find out more about Forest Villa MB ›

Double Courtyard House, New Zealand, by Roberts Gray Architects

Rammed earth was used to form the low-slung Double Courtyard House, designed Roberts Gray Architects on a sand dune near Auckland.

Within its heavy walls are two contrasting courtyards – one shaded and one exposed to sun – around which the living spaces are organised, giving the home its name.

Find out more about Double Courtyard House ›

Casa Diez Pies, Mexico, by Studio Font

Casa Diez Pies was conceived as a series of stepped terraces, supported by 10 chunky concrete columns, which descend a coastal cliff in Mazunte.

The 10 supports, which give the home its name Casa Diez Pies or Ten-Foot House, were designed to minimise the impact on the site while creating spaces for staircases, bathrooms and storage spaces.

Find out more about Casa Diez Pies ›

Splitscape Residence, India, by SpaceDNA

This multi-generational house in India is organised across split-level floors and an orange staircase, encased by facades of perforated steel screens.

The jaali-like screens filter light into the home, including a triple-height living space at its heart, while allowing natural ventilation and creating a sense of openness.

"The interior design was intentionally kept minimal so that spatial experience, light and materiality could take centre stage," the studio told Dezeen.

Find out more about Splitscape Residence ›

This week on Dezeen, we unveiled a pair of slides that heat up and vibrate feet to help athlete's recover.

Created by sportswear company Nike and health technology company Hyperice, the slides contain a device in their straps that can heat and massage the top of feet.

Continuing our Future Stadium series we investigated why stadiums are becoming more outlandish and impactful.

To conclude the series, we rounded up the world's record-breaking stadiums including, the biggest and the most expensive.

In architecture news, we revealed that the long-awaited Guggenheim Abu Dhabi museum, designed by the late Frank Gehry, is finally set to open in December.

The museum will become the latest attraction on Saadiyat Island, alongside Foster + Partners' Zayed National Museum, Mecanoo's National History Museum and Jean Nouvel's Louvre Abu Dhabi.

Following the news that the Glasgow School of Art cannot afford to renovate the Mackintosh Building after two major fires, Rory Olcayto suggested the institution give up the building in an opinion on Dezeen.

"We should rebuild the Mackintosh Building without the Glasgow School of Art – it has clearly exhausted its mandate as steward," he said.

While the future of Charles Rennie Mackintosh's best-known work remains very uncertain, numerous other significant building were protected this week as UNESCO added several additions to its World Heritage List.

In total, 13 modernist buildings in Finland designed by architects Aino, Elissa and Alvar Aalto were added to the list along with a collection of 10 Soviet modernist buildings in Tashkent, Uzbekistan.

In North America, a bridge connecting the United States and Canada opened to the public this week.

Named after Canadian-born Detroit Red Wings hockey player Gordie Howe, the design of the curved bridge was informed by a hockey slapshot.

Popular projects this week included a public toilet in Japan topped with a sweeping timber canopy, a charred wood house in Vermont and a relaunched 1986 Dieter Rams door handle.

Listen to our journalists talk about the key design and architecture stories of the past seven days on our Dezeen Weekly podcast, which this week focused on the new, world's tallest timber building.

item.content:encoded:
New York City studio Martin Hopp Architect has completed a building with a mass-timber structure for a school in Hempstead, New York, prioritising healthy living spaces and materials on a tight budget.

Evergreen Charter School opened in 2025 on a suburban site on Long Island in New York state. The K-12 school comprises 89,000 square feet (8,270 square metres) of conditioned space and 106,000 square feet (9,850 square metres) of non-conditioned space and prioritises healthy, resilient learning environments.

"From the outset, we focused on creating high-performance spaces filled with daylight, fresh air and natural materials – environments that would actively support students' wellbeing and concentration," said studio founder Martin Hopp.

"With a very limited budget, we made a deliberate decision to pursue a 'most from least' approach."

The studio invested in performance with a mass timber structure, efficient systems, durable materials and flexible classrooms that can change over time to meet the school's needs.

"The ambition was not spectacle, but generosity – to demonstrate that even under tight constraints, a school building can be uplifting, responsible and deeply supportive of learning," Hopp said.

The limited footprint prompted the team to divide the building into two volumes with a slot carved through the massing that allows daylight to reach deep into the plan.

The circulation spine aligns with the junction of the two volumes, allowing cross views across the five floors.

"In this way, the layout balances efficiency with environmental performance," the studio said.

"The compact footprint maximizes usable space on the site, while the split massing strategy prioritizes daylight, ventilation and a strong sense of spatial organization for students and staff."

The whole school was designed around a classroom model that prioritised natural light, acoustics, thermal comfort and indoor air quality.

In addition to the structure that reduces the building's embodied carbon, mass timber is used throughout the entire building as the finish material, adding warmth, texture, and visual calm to the environment.

On the exterior, timber shading devices run in long fins up the primary facade, providing a warm, natural contrast to the grey cementitious panels. Above the upper enclosed floor, a timber pergola topped with solar arrays shades the rooftop soccer pitch.

Inside, the ceilings of the classrooms, gymnasium and cafeteria are partially exposed mass timber, while acoustic ceiling panels help maintain noise levels.

Read:

AMMA completes mass-timber modular school "that breathes" in Barbados

The project is tracking toward LEED Platinum certification with a range of passive and active sustainability strategies.

"Together, these passive and active systems reinforce the project's core ambition," the studio said. "To create a high-performance learning environment that reduces operational costs while supporting student health and environmental awareness."

Mass timber architecture has spread to education architecture over the last several years with projects like the University of Arkansas' architecture and design school by Grafton Architects, a treehouse-like social hub at Harvard University by Studio Gang and a lantern-like research centre for the University of Toronto by Montgomery Sisam Architects.

The photography is by Frank Oudeman.

item.content:encoded:
A horizontal glass skybridge connects residential and office skyscrapers at this project by Königsberger Vannucchi Arquitetos Associados in São Paulo to preserve the "individual reading of each tower while simultaneously reinforcing their unity".

Located in São Paulo as part of the larger Eixo Platina mixed-use development by developer Porte Engenharia e Urbanism, the Almagah 227 skyscrapers were designed to respond to demand for commercial and corporate spaces in the city's East Zone.

Almagah 227 consists of one 25-floor residential tower and one 27-floor office tower. They are linked by the skybridge on the 13th through 14th floor, which contrasts the towers' warm, porcelain facade with dark glazing.

"By articulating the two buildings, the bridge preserves the individual reading of each tower while simultaneously reinforcing their unity as a single ensemble," said Königsberger Vannucchi Arquitetos Associados."It expands the functional integration of the development and consolidates the identity of the complex."

The buildings also stand on a broad, glass base that is clad in the same dark glazing as the bridge above. At the bottom of the residential skyscraper, the platform runs into a large pool deck and recreation area.

Along the entirety of the ground floor, the base contains commercial spaces, while the 2nd and 3rd floors contain open-plan coworking areas.

The bridge itself contains corporate programming, along with a restaurant, while the residential tower includes "compact" and studio apartments.

The studio said the facade was constructed using a ventilated facade system, which contains a small gap between its porcelain cladding and the masonry structure.

Read:

Nitsche Arquitetos integrates timber kiosks into São Paulo metro station renovations

Constant air circulating through this space removes "approximately 20 per cent" of absorbed heat, according to the team, while the system also allowed expedited construction time, reduced waste generation and "less maintenance".

As part of the broader Eixo Platina masterplan, the area is intended to provide mixed-use programming in São Paulo's dense East Zone. It contains several skyscrapers along a broad strip in the city, some of which have already been completed.

"Almagah 227 reflects the core principles of Eixo Platina by incorporating programmatic diversity, strong integration with its surroundings and architectural solutions that enhance the city."

"The complex stems from the same principle that structures the entire masterplan: bringing housing, work and leisure into closer proximity, reducing daily commutes and qualifying the urban environment through diverse and connected infrastructure," said the studio.

Elsewhere in the city, Königsberger Vannucchi Arquitetos Associados completed a skyscraper with porcelain and wood cladding, while FGMF Arquitetos completed a pixelated skyscraper in the Pinheiros district.

item.content:encoded:
British studio Charles Gillespie Architecture has completed The Linhay, a family house in rural Somerset wrapped by a deep concrete colonnade that provides sheltered nesting spaces for birds.

Designed by the studio's founder Charles Gillespie for himself and his young family, the house draws on the traditional linhay – an agricultural barn found across Somerset and Devon with a distinctive open-fronted form.

Rather than recreating the historic building type, the studio translated its defining characteristics into a full-length colonnade formed from precast concrete columns.

Behind this row of precast concrete columns is a sheltered terrace, which leads directly to main living spaces through large glazed openings. The recessed facade blocks high summer sun and admits lower winter light.

The cylindrical columns reference the historic linhay barns, where rounded supports made it easier for livestock to pass through the open-fronted structures, while giving the facade a regular rhythm.

Bird and bat boxes, bee bricks and nesting spaces are integrated into this area, allowing it to double as habitat for local wildlife.

"The colonnade gives the house its identity, controls sunlight, extends the living space and provides shelter for wildlife," Gillespie told Dezeen.

"Environmental performance, biodiversity and architectural character do not need to be separate ambitions."

Gillespie recalled that the distinctive structure initially sparked some confusion among neighbours during construction.

"The precast colonnade was erected quite early during the build," Gillespie said. "I'd say our neighbours had a bit of a shock, perhaps with the fear we were building some kind of Greek revival building in the middle of a field!"

Read:

Forgeworks revamps Somerset farmhouse with low-lying stone extension

The two-storey home sits on West Farm in Babcary as part of an intergenerational development that also includes Highlands, a second house for Gillespie's parents.

Together, the buildings replace a collection of former agricultural outbuildings while allowing three generations of the same family to live independently on the same site.

Gillespie described the arrangement as a "family campus", with the two houses connected by shared gardens and daily routines while remaining separate homes.

From the approach, the Linhay resembles a deliberately simple pitched-roof farmhouse combining pale stone with vertical timber cladding.

A lower wing with an intensive green roof extends into the former farmyard, creating the impression that part of the surrounding field has been folded over the building.

Inside, the home is organised around an open-plan kitchen, dining and play space that projects into the garden, giving it views in three directions across meadow planting and surrounding fields.

Exposed timber ceiling beams, lime-plastered walls, polished concrete floors and cherry timber joinery create a restrained material palette, punctuated by a pink pigmented concrete staircase.

Timber was sourced from the nearby Stourhead estate, while the stone came from a quarry seven miles from the site.

Around the house, meadow planting, an orchard and pollinator-friendly species replace areas of former hardstanding.

The green roof and surrounding planting are intended to strengthen biodiversity across the farmstead.

The all-electric home combines passive environmental strategies with an air-source heat pump, mechanical ventilation with heat recovery and rooftop photovoltaic panels.

Charles Gillespie Architecture was founded by Gillespie in 2024 in Castle Cary, Somerset. The studio focuses on homes and rural projects, with The Linhay and the neighbouring Highlands house among its first completed works.

Other British houses recently featured on Dezeen include the brick-clad Skylark home, for which House of EM referenced mid-century design principles, and Westview Cottage in Dungeness, which Hollaway Studio completed with a monochrome palette.

The photography is by Dave Watts.

item.content:encoded:
Certification company Bureau Veritas has launched the UK Net Zero Carbon Buildings Standard, a voluntary verification scheme that determines a building's carbon performance.

Now open for submissions, the UK Net Zero Carbon Buildings Standard assesses net-zero claims of buildings against an industry-agreed definition, aiming to minimise greenwashing.

New buildings, existing buildings and retrofit projects can be entered voluntarily to the standard, which grants a Net Zero Carbon Aligned verification to buildings that meet the set criteria.

Verification requires 12 months of in-use building data

Buildings submitted to the scheme will be assessed by Bureau Veritas based on 12 months of in-use energy data and as-built upfront embodied-carbon data.

To be verified as Net Zero Carbon Aligned, buildings must remove on-site fossil fuels, generate on-site renewable energy and minimise the upfront embodied carbon and measured in-use energy consumption.

Offsets cannot be used to meet any of the required limits, but can be considered to tackle residual carbon when mandatory requirements are met.

Standard "marks a pivotal shift in the industry"

Bureau Veritas hopes that providing a set standard for net zero in the building industry will build credibility in carbon claims, shifting the focus from design-stage modelling data to in-use performance.

"The launch of verification under the UK Net Zero Carbon Buildings Standard marks a pivotal shift in the industry, moving from predicted outcomes to measured, independently verified in-use performance," said Bureau Veritas vice president Antoine Giros.

"As verification administrator, Bureau Veritas will ensure that net-zero claims are accurate, reliable, and backed by rigorous assessment," he continued. "Our role is to provide independent expertise in building performance and carbon assessment, to give investors, occupiers, and stakeholders genuine confidence in building performance."

"With nearly 200 years of credibility in testing, inspection and certification, we're proud to support the industry's transition towards a low-carbon future."

Read:

"It's time to see all those circular economy strategies for what they are"

Prior to final verification, buildings can undergo a verified check at the practical completion stage to gauge whether they are on track to meet the standards when in use.

Bureau Veritas also provides a carbon performance evaluation for buildings that do not meet all the requirements for Net Zero Carbon Aligned verification, to track their decarbonisation progress.

"It is now only a matter of time before the first buildings are verified as Net Zero Carbon Aligned," said UK Net Zero Carbon Buildings Standard CEO Katie Jackson-Clements.

"These front-runners will represent environmental leadership within the UK built environment industry and pave the way for many more verifications to follow."

Sustainable buildings that have recently featured on Dezeen include a net-zero campus in Washington for the American Institute of Architects and a house in the Hamptons designed to be net-positive-energy.

item.content:encoded:
In this week's comments update, readers are discussing Yano Aoyama Architecture Design's public toilet for the Tobe Zoological Park in Ehime Prefecture, Japan.

Comprising a pair of sculpted concrete blocks topped by a naturally curved cedar roof, the design of the public bathroom cubicles draws from the zoo's wooded surroundings.

"Simple, beautiful forms"

Commenters were on the same page, doling out high praise for the Japanese public toilet.

"This is powerful, correct, elegant, vaguely historical, well-made... I could go on," wrote Ben.

Pa Varreon agreed, saying, "Very much elegant. I would almost travel to Japan to visit and use these facilities."

"Simple, beautiful forms," remarked Steve Hassler. "Thanks for this."

Andy Enock wrote, "Japan takes this seriously; they have some brilliant designs."

"It is magnificent and beautiful, I wish we could have something like this in the USA," wrote Joaquin. "Pay here is not the same as pee here, people," he added.

What are your thoughts? Join the discussion ›

"The 90s called and asked for their clunky designs back"

Another story gaining traction this week was the North Tower skyscraper in Chicago by architecture studio SOM, which features a series of cascading terraces.

"I actually like the 80s throwback to geometric play," said Frank Lloyd Wrong.

In accord, Layla wrote, "This is a great contrast to the confused hodge-podge of residential buildings on the other side of the river. Looks good to me!"

"This is much more interesting than the typical glass box condo tower with wafer balconies," said Fremp. "It's like a new take on a classic art deco massing. Great addition to the Chicago skyline."

"Sleek and sane!" said Blau.

Other commenters weren't so keen.

"The 90s called and asked for their clunky designs back," wrote RK. "'Tired skyscraper' would have been a more apt article headline."

Luc Helterbrand said, "In person this building appears very heavy and clumsy. Disappointing addition to the skyline of this great city."

"It's not finished, but I doubt it will look better when it is," wrote This is not Hank in agreement.

Have you had your say yet? Join the discussion ›

"1970s inspired tower with beaver chew"

A project that intrigued readers was the Atlassian Central skyscraper in Sydney by SHoP Architects and BVN Architecture, which has become the world's tallest hybrid timber tower.

"Appropriate then that the shape resembles a tree about to be felled," said Jim Angrabright.

Milton Welch responded to this, calling it a "1970s inspired tower with beaver chew".

"Intrigued by the structure, but also the final enclosure," wrote JZ. "As far as high-rises go, it appears to have its own unique, coherent and tasteful resolution."

"Looking good," agreed Matthew. "But those slanted glazings are providing fantastic ledges for pigeons."

Though replies were overwhelmingly positive, some commenters expressed doubts.

"Where is the heavy timber shipped from? Do they consider this travel distance in the calculations of the amount of embodied energy?" asked DEvODA. "Sometimes these things are all show and no real benefit."

"What staggers me is the sheer volume of the voids around the intriguing internal wooden floors and walls," wrote John. "What purpose do these spaces serve?"

Just as unimpressed, Tom Roberts said, "Who cares what it is made of, it is an ugly and unbalanced design."

What do you reckon? Join the discussion ›

Keep up to date on the latest discussions on our comments page and subscribe to our weekly Debate newsletter, where we feature the best reader comments from stories in the past seven days.

item.content:encoded:
One message for humans and another for artificial intelligence are contained in the letters of Decoy Font, made by the company Mixfont for those who want to avoid having their data scraped.

Decoy Font makes use of a well-known optical illusion to trick contemporary artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots into misreading messages.

The font features two layers of image – one in thin but clear outlines in the foreground, and another in blurry dark shapes in the background.

Humans can read both letterforms by shifting focus, squinting, or moving further or closer to the screen, but usually see the dark letters in the background more vividly.

However, current large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT, which work by reading the pixels of an image up close, automatically read the less visible, crisply outlined forms in the foreground, Mixfont founder and AI researcher Eric Lu explained.

Lu created Decoy Font and a similar earlier experiment, Ghost Font, which obscures messages in moving animations, to explore the potential of "anti-AI" fonts to protect text from being scraped or read by LLMs.

At the same time, he wanted to more open-endedly explore the limits of AI perception and how quickly they are changing, in line with Mixfont's AI-led business. The digital font foundry and research lab offers AI-powered products such as a text-to-image font generator.

"In my work at Mixfont I've been researching ways that AI and typography intersect," he told Dezeen. "I tested many different techniques [to create an anti-AI font], including Ghost Font to test the limits of what LLMs would easily solve."

"Decoy Font emerged out of these attempts as an effective try – the idea that we could combine two letters that are readable in different ways proved to be difficult for AI models to reason about clearly."

Lu demonstrated the effectiveness of Decoy Font on Mixfont's blog with screenshots that show him fooling the advanced models GPT-5.6 Sol and Gemini 3.5  with an image that to humans clearly reads "sleep early". Both models pronounced that the image says "binge shows".

Other examples on the blog include text that says "day dream" for humans and "pay bills" for AI, or "happy human" for humans and "sorry robot" for AI.

Decoy Font can be used either as a web application that encodes specific hidden messages or as a downloadable TTF font file, which produces text that AI will perceive as gibberish. This gibberish text triggers suspicion from some chatbots and suggestions that it could help analyse it.

The technique behind Decoy Font is that of the "hybrid image", where an image with a low spatial frequency – usually typified by big shapes, flat tones and broad gradients – is combined with another with a high spatial frequency, usually with edges, fine lines and noise.

It is most famously demonstrated in an image of Marilyn Monroe that, up close, looks like Albert Einstein. There are also examples of textual hybrid images.

Mixfont created Decoy Font using their own code and the public domain font DejaVu Sans Mono as a reference for the background letterforms.

Read:

Eight actually interesting uses of AI from 2025

Lu told Dezeen that it took many iterations to get the right balance of line thickness, blurriness and letter spacing to optimise readability, and that Mixfont also experimented with red and blue colours before settling on grey as the most legible and effective choice.

In addition to being used for private messaging, Lu thinks Decoy Font could have applications for technologies like CAPTCHA, where simple tests are used to determine if a computer user is human.

He also considers the project to be a useful conversation starter around issues of AI and public trust, even if the technology's rapid advancement means it may not have practical value for long.

"It started as an exploration of how AI and typography intersect, but it was also meant to raise awareness of the growing reach and capabilities of AI," said Lu. "I think the reaction to the font shows that there are many folks who feel strong AI fatigue, and want a way to defend themselves against the presence of AI in their lives."

"In practical terms, however, I think it's important as a benchmark today.," Lu continued.

"AI might not be able to read Decoy Font (at least at first glance) today, but it's possible that in just a few months it will be able to read it easily. Tracking this progress will be interesting to see."

Another recent project to look critically at AI is Domenico di Paolo and Kieran Feechan's Imago audio player, which suggests a creative alternative to commercial AI music systems with scraped training data.

item.content:encoded:
German architecture studio Holzrausch drew inspiration from cinematic interiors when designing this townhouse in Munich, which combines dark wood with natural stone and lush tropical planting.

The clients for the Private Club project are film producer Cornelia Popp and her husband, who created a storyboard evoking 1970s South American movies as inspiration for the project.

Instead of a typical bright and minimalist German aesthetic, Holzrausch leaned into the darker, secluded and more theatrical atmosphere presented to them by the couple.

"The house isn't experienced all at once – it unfolds scene by scene," Holzrausch co-founder Sven Petzold told Dezeen.

"Every transition, every change of light and every material is part of a spatial narrative that makes the home feel immersive rather than simply functional."

A carefully chosen material palette combined with ambient lighting contributes to the interior's moody, club-like feel, while the extensive use of wood and plants introduces a sense of natural comfort.

The townhouse is located within a typical 1990s development with no strong architectural identity. Instead of responding to this context, the architects chose to give the home a distinct style that is unrelated to its surroundings.

"We wanted the architecture to disappear into the background so that atmosphere, light and material become the defining experience," Petzold added.

A small vestibule and a narrow wood-panelled staircase, envisioned by the architects as a kind of gorge, form a dramatic entry sequence that culminates in the bright, naturally lit living space.

The double-height room features large glazed doors that open onto a balcony, along with clerestory windows that allow daylight to filter through plants arranged along the top of the built-in cabinetry.

Joinery throughout the home is crafted from smoked oak, which complements the dark-stained okoume wood floors. A wood-panelled ceiling contributes to the cohesive, tonal aesthetic.

"The deliberate use of darker materials creates a sense of intimacy and a club-like atmosphere – almost like a refined, contemporary cave," said Petzold.

"The enveloping tones absorb light, add depth and warmth, and create a calm, immersive environment that feels both protective and inviting."

In the kitchen and bathrooms, the warm wood meets cooler and smoother materials such as Vitoria Regia quartzite, Wachenzeller limestone, stainless steel and coloured glass.

The kitchen's marbled quartzite backsplash and countertop catch the eye, along with pops of vibrant yellow provided by the bar stools, dining table and cabinets, contained in a niche that functions as a pantry.

Read:

Kéré Architecture creates "vertical playground" for kindergarten at Technical University of Munich

The central island is fabricated from stainless steel, which introduces a cool and precise contrast to the wood. The metal's brushed finish subtly reflects light and movement within the space.

Holzrausch sourced all of the furniture, lighting, textiles and plants for the home.

The interior features bespoke carpentry, joinery and furniture crafted by Holzrausch in its own workshop, along with selected pieces by Dimore Milano, Tacchini, Haymann and vintage Pierre Chareau.

Holzrausch was founded in Munich in 1998 by Sven Petzold and Tobias Petri.

Previous projects from Holzrausch include a penthouse in Frankfurt with living spaces that open onto a large terrace.

The studio has also created a holiday home in Mallorca informed by the colourful style of Mexican architect Luis Barragán.

The photography is courtesy of Holzrausch.

item.content:encoded:
The husband-and-wife founders of California studio SPF Architects have renovated their octagonal house in the Santa Monica Mountains and added elements to protect it against wildfire.

Called the Mountain Residence, the project involved the renovation and redesign of a 1980s house that sits on a 17-acre (6.9-hectare) site in Los Angeles County.

When Zoltan Pali and Judit Fekete-Pali, founders of SPF Architects, purchased the home, they knew they wanted to overhaul it.

Octagonal in plan, the house had stucco cladding, outdated interior finishes, heavy ornamentation, and a compartmentalised layout.

"The goal was to simplify and modernise the original house while working within its unusual octagonal footprint," said Zoltan Pali, who co-founded his studio in 1995.

"Rather than attempting to alter the home's geometry, the design embraced it."

The couple and their team embarked on a massive overhaul that would improve functionality, strengthen connections between inside and out, and bolster the structure's ability to withstand wildfire.

The house was stripped down to its structural frame and rebuilt.

On the exterior, the building envelope was reconstructed using "a layered assembly" that enhances thermal performance and fire resistance.

The assembly consists of existing stucco, furring strips, rigid insulation, gypsum sheathing and a vapour barrier. The outer surface is clad in a continuous layer of Class A, fire-resistant asphalt shingles.

"The shingles extend across both the walls and roof, creating a unified exterior expression and a continuous protective shell around the residence," the team said.

Outdated windows were replaced with high-performance glazing, and openings were enlarged in certain areas.

In addition to the asphalt shingles, the team incorporated fire-protection measures such as exterior fire sprinklers, supplemental water storage tanks, backup generators and "defensible landscape strategies".

"Together, these systems provide both passive and active protection measures designed to support the home's long-term performance in a high-fire-risk environment," the team said.

The project also entailed structural upgrades, such as the addition of shear walls and moment frames to "strengthen the building's lateral stability and seismic performance".

Within the home, the layout was reconfigured to create better flow and sight lines.

"Compartmentalised spaces were reconfigured to create a more open floor plan while preserving the home's distinctive geometry," the team said.

"Several walls and three fireplaces were removed, hallways were eliminated, and the floor plan was opened up to create more connected living spaces."

On the ground level, social spaces were moved to the centre of the home, while bedrooms were placed on the perimeter.

The upper level, which formerly held a family room, now contains the primary suite and an architectural studio for 20 people.

Read:

SPF Architects clads cantilevered Beverly Hills house in black and bronze panels

New interior finishes include Douglas fir, which is found throughout the residence. The house has ample space for Pali and Fekete-Pali's art collection.

"The house does not have all the wall area for some of our largest pieces, but we created enough wall space for us to enjoy the lion's share of what we accumulated over the years," the team said.

While the couple initially envisioned the space being a main office for their architecture firm, most of their employees and collaborators prefer to work at their Culver City office because it is closer to their homes.

In turn, the Mountain Residence has become a retreat-like space used for occasional design sessions, in addition to being the couple's primary dwelling.

"The renovation transformed what had been a highly compartmentalised and ornamented interior into a more restrained, light-filled environment rooted in geometry, natural materials and views of the site," they said.

Other projects by SPF Architects include a cantilevering Beverly Hills house clad in black and bronze aluminium and a three-winged residence that stretches across a hilltop in LA's Bel Aire neighbourhood.

The photography is by Renzo Pali.

item.content:encoded:
Architecture studio HOK has released designs for Bank of America Stadium in North Carolina featuring a new facade treatment and luxurious amenity spaces to "meet the expectations of fans and athletes for decades to come".

Tepper Sports & Entertainment, owner of the stadium, commissioned HOK to revamp the 75,000-seat Bank of America Stadium. It was originally designed by Wagner Murray Architects and Populous (then HOK Sport) and opened in 1996.

The architecture studio highlighted the decision to renovate rather than replace the stadium, the latter a move that many teams are making as they seek to create facilities better suited to year-round operation.

"Rather than replace the venue, the renovation of Bank of America Stadium aims to modernize one of the NFL's most recognizable stadiums and ensure it continues to meet the expectations of fans and athletes for decades to come," said HOK.

HOK's exterior intervention will be most visible where the concrete bowl is visible above the exterior shell. The current configuration features a series of concrete arches at the bowl's crest, resembling a crown, in line with Charlotte's moniker – Queen City.

The new crown will be smoother, with metallic bands wrapping the arches.

Below, a roof will wrap the stadium's current exterior mezzanine, while the domes that crest the entrance arches will be converted into blocky forms. The remainder of the facade will be covered in glass, obscuring the columns and spandrels visible on the current facade.

Amenity spaces are top of mind for the redevelopment, with a new social patio at the top of the stands as well as improved and expanded gathering spaces and athletic facilities.

Renderings show a lounge with white walls and a modern chandelier in a double-height space with a mezzanine looking down.

HOK said the redesign was meant to draw from the locale without being "overtly thematic".

"Drawing inspiration from the landscapes and culture of the Carolinas, the design establishes a strong sense of place through materiality, texture and restrained detailing rather than overt thematic expression," said HOK.

"Interior environments subtly reflect the region's mountain, coastal, urban and local identities. A clean, forward-looking palette of metal, glass and wood with refined finishes inside and out creates a contemporary architectural language designed to endure for decades."

Read:

Renovation of problematic Montreal Olympic Stadium roof keeps "original intention" in mind

Landscaping new public plazas will be integrated into the area surrounding the stadium, as well as an entertainment venue that will be able to seat more than 4,000 people. The entertainment venue is a boxy structure attached to the stadium and is not part of HOK's scope.

HOK said these moves were aimed at making the stadium more public-facing.

"Strategic interventions, including new public plazas, social gathering spaces, park-like landscaping and ground-level activation, transform a once inward-facing facility into a transparent multi-use environment, reinforcing the stadium's important role in the community," said the studio.

Groundbreaking is planned for 2027, with the team saying it plans on keeping the building operational during renovations.

Dezeen recently launched a series called Future Stadium that examines the past, present and future of stadium design worldwide.

In other NFL news, the Kansas City Chiefs recently announced a new Populous-designed stadium.

item.content:encoded:
US president Donald Trump has unveiled conceptual renderings for an overhaul of Dulles International Airport in Washington DC, with a design that builds on top of architect Eero Saarinen's famous terminal building.

Yesterday, the US Department of Transportation (DOT) announced the plan in partnership with The Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority and United Airlines, after dozens of architecture studios including ZHA and Adjaye Associates submitted proposals to an RFI from the government late last year.

Trump said he selected the designs "after an extensive review of more than 30 proposals with the top architects anywhere in the world".

However, no architecture studios is explicitly attached to the project at present and a spokesperson from United Airlines told Dezeen that the conceptual renderings could be attributed to their organisation.

"The Airports Authority and United will partner on this transformation to reshape many aspects of the Dulles journey, with new and modernized facilities designed to create a smoother, more efficient and elevated experience from curb to gate, while preserving architect Eero Saarinen's iconic main terminal design," said United Airlines.

The renderings show a sloped structure with clerestory glass directly attached to the columned Saarinen design. Sloped arms on either side of the main terminal will extend outwards while new facilities will be added including a parking garage Trump said will be "the largest garage in the world", according to NBC News.

According to the DOT, the project scope will add 5 million square feet (464,515 square metres) of additional space to the airport.

It will include enhancing the entry with new check-in facilities, "building new and modernized concourses" and replacing the C and D concourses, while installing tunnels to replace the "people movers" – trams that transported people between concourses.

The DOT said the project will be completed over the next "several years" and announced an increase of as much as $13 billion to the original renovation funds.

"The investment of more than $20 billion represents a significant increase over the $7 billion previously allocated for the Dulles modernization program," said the DOT.

"MWAA, working with airlines serving Dulles, will finance the new concourses and terminal facilities through municipal bonds, which offer significantly lower interest rates than bonds available to private-sector firms."

Read:

Flurry of famed architects submit designs for Trump airport terminal

The design comes after a masterplan was announced by the airport in July of last year.

In December, Trump called Dulles "incorrectly designed" and a "terrible airport", though he did compliment the design of the main terminal designed by Saarinen in the 1960s.

The DOT did not respond to Dezeen's request for comment.

The images are courtesy of United Airlines.

item.content:encoded:
Dezeen School Shows: a clothing line informed by hip-hop music and the work of fashion designer Dapper Dan is among projects from the Lebanese American University.

Also featured are handover pieces designed to reflect Pakistani culture and clothing that takes inspiration from sculptor John Chamberlain's creations.

Lebanese American University

Institution: School of Architecture and Design
Course: B.F.A. in Fashion Design
Tutors: Jurgi Persoons, Jalal Moghraby and Ana Har

School statement:

"This year, the Lebanese American University (LAU) celebrated its 10th graduating cohort in fashion design, marking a decade of cultivating emerging talent through the School of Architecture and Design's Fashion Design Program, developed in collaboration with renowned Lebanese fashion designer Elie Saab.

"Combining rigour with creative exploration and critical inquiry, the program encourages students to engage with fashion as both a global industry and a cultural practice.

"Titled Ten, the 2026 graduate show reflected on a decade of growth while considering what it means to create fashion during a time of uncertainty and transformation.

"In a world driven by data, fashion remains a deeply human industry of measurements and economics, yet equally a space for emotion, identity and memory.

"For this graduating cohort – mentored by Jurgi Persoons, Jalal Moghraby and Ana Har – design became an act of presence. A way of reclaiming hope, agency and the power of imagining what comes next despite months of a raging war in Lebanon and the Levant that left scores of students displaced and homeless.

"Ten marked a milestone achieved against all odds. Ten – a perfect number – may be a threshold, but it certainly is not a limit."

Rogue by Malak Al Ayyash

"Taking home the coveted Prix du Jury, which includes a six-month internship at the Elie Saab studios in Beirut, Lebanon, Ayyash's collection explores the tension between the human body – namely the female body – and the constructed ideals that have historically governed it.

"Satirically fashioned through architectural silhouettes inspired by dolls, both infantile and grotesque, the collection challenges human expectations surrounding representation and conventional perceptions of propriety."

Student: Malak Al Ayyash
Email: malak.alayyash[at]lau.edu

The Fall by Reem Daher

"Winner of the Excellence in Craftsmanship award, Daher meticulously hand-wove an entire collection informed by a reflection on identity, emotion and social structure in Pakistani society.

"Through myth-inspired storytelling based on Adam and Eve, each piece symbolises a creature of feeling, revealing how power, labour and culture define the human experience in the age of AI."

Student: Reem Daher
Email: reem.daher02[at]lau.edu

Manifesto for the Post-Apocalyptic Lover by Myriam Atallah

"Recipient of the Excellence in Concept Development award, Atallah's collection evokes the aftermath of the world, where garments become obsolete relics: costumes performed into the void, severed from function, gender and the gaze of the other.

"Her collection imagines dressing as an act of solitary delirium – a surreal self-entertainment staged for no audience but the self and the ether.

"Amidst ruin, the body adorns itself in absurdity, as if performance persists long after humanity has disappeared."

Student: Myriam Atallah
Email: myriam.atallah[at]lau.edu

Fake Replica by Lea Fares

"Receiving the Excellence in Construction and Technique award, Fares' collection explores how we have all turned into dandies in the age of social media.

"Existing in a state of artificial sublimation, identity is formed behind the screen. The flattened garments become a facade of identity, while the back reveals the hidden reality behind the image."

Student: Lea Fares
Email: lea.fares02[at]lau.edu

Brushing Shoulders by Elias Makhoul

"Winner of the Coup de Coeur award, this collection questions who has the authority to define good taste in the contemporary era.

"Inspired by John Chamberlain's sculptures from discarded car parts, the collection is fashioned around fictitious narratives and imaginings of interactions of strangers in the streets, pushing the idea of individuals exchanging not only feelings but parts of themselves through garments, textures and physique."

Student: Elias Makhoul
Email: elias.makhoul[at]lau.edu

Ctrl C by Reem Hennaoui

"'Man is an imitative creature.' – Aristotle.

"Ctrl C explores the instinct to disappear into the crowd, to imitate, repeat and blend in as a method of survival. Superposing patterns of urban archetypes to create novel and unpredictable realities, where familiar is shielded in the arbitrary."

Student: Reem Hennaoui
Email: reem.hennaoui[at]lau.edu

The Innocent Gaze by Lea Kelechian

"Kelechian's collection explores unlearning, letting go of conventions in fashion to view the world through a child's eyes, as per Jonathan Fineberg.

"The garments were designed intuitively, abandoning traditional techniques in favour of free-form draping inspired by children's drawings that Kelechian had collected with the help of her kindergarten teacher."

Student: Lea Kelechian
Email: lea.kelechian[at]lau.edu

Antithesis by Alex Kassardjian

"Antithesis explores the tension between desire and restraint, questioning the visual codes through which power, masculinity and attraction are constructed

"Drawing on masculine iconography and the language of fetishism, the collection subverts familiar symbols to challenge conventional notions of desirability.

"Rather than celebrating excess, it proposes restraint as a conscious act, examining how societies regulate desire through expectations of propriety, discipline and self-control."

Student: Alex Kassardjian
Email: alex.kassardjian[at]lau.edu

Smells Like Bloomsbury by Hanin Bzeih

"Bzeih's collection traces the recurring struggles experienced by artists across different eras, backgrounds and social contexts, exploring the complex relationship between creativity, vulnerability and psychological turmoil.

"Through references to figures such as Virginia Woolf and Kurt Cobain, it reflects on how vastly different lives can be shaped by shared experiences of isolation, emotional intensity and inner conflict, questioning the pressures placed upon artistic expression and the human condition."

Student: Hanin Bzeih
Email: hanin.bzeih[at]lau.edu

Trap Époque by Farah Alawiye

"Drawing from the bold visual language of hip-hop culture and the pioneering legacy of Dapper Dan, this collection reinterprets streetwear through the lens of classical luxury.

"References to iconic fashion houses are balanced with timeless expressions of feminine elegance, shaped by Alawiye's upbringing and exposure to fashion through her mother, a stylist who instilled in her an appreciation for refined craftsmanship."

Student: Farah Alawiye
Email: farah.alawiye[at]lau.edu

Photography is by Tarek Moukaddem.

item.content:encoded:
﻿Local architecture studio DoDesign has completed the Nanhai Buddha Pavilion in Chongqing, China, creating a shelter with gridded metal walls that are filled with thousands of loose cedar logs.

The origins of the pavilion lay in the discovery of a Ming-dynasty Buddhist shrine on the site – a wooded hill near Nanhai Village – which the owner marked with a Buddha sculpture carved into the large trunk of a crape myrtle tree.

This sculpture has since become a local pilgrimage site, but after a shed-like structure housing it proved insufficient at sheltering it from the sun and rain, DoDesign was commissioned to create a new pavilion.

Rather than designing a more traditional structure, the studio designed a pared-back shelter, lined with thousands of small cedar logs inserted into its gridded metal walls with which visitors could interact and rearrange.

"From the beginning, the intention was never to create an elevated religious monument," said the studio.

"Instead, we hoped to make a place where the spirit could quietly settle – a space capable of holding both devotion and everyday life," it added.

Black-steel columns support the gridded timber roof of Nanhai Buddha Pavilion, with partitions and shaded spaces created by standalone walls made from welded grids of black-steel rods.

While around 4,000 of these small logs were cut – enough to fill the walls of the entire structure – only half have been put into place, with visitors invited to place the remainder and rearrange them as they see fit.

Read:

Liz Gálvez "reframes" air conditioning with shade pavilion in Los Angeles

According to DoDesign, both this interactivity and the weathering of the cedar wood over time represent an "exploration into change and indeterminacy" that was informed by the teachings of Buddhism.

"Wood remains unfixed, walls continue to weather, light constantly drifts, and people themselves complete the architecture through participation," it said.

"Perhaps the true meaning of this pavilion lies in becoming a gentle medium through which people may, amid impermanence, briefly encounter their own Buddha-nature," added the studio.

Atop the pavilion, the flat timber roof shelters the Buddha sculpture and has also been given a black finish, with skylights at both its centre and in a band close to the perimeter allowing daylight to enter.

Previous projects by DoDesign include the Drifting Stones Pavilion, also in Chongquing, for which the studio concealed a glazed viewpoint beneath a stepped stack of imitation stones designed to blend with the surrounding rocky site.

Other pavilions recently featured on Dezeen include a barrel-vaulted community greenhouse at the Barbican in London and a structure formed of cord and earthen blocks in Los Angeles to showcase the potential of urban shade.

The photography is courtesy of DoDesign.

item.content:encoded:
Stadiums are often vying to be record-breaking structures. To conclude our Future Stadium series, we look at those that top the lists, from the biggest and tallest to the most expensive.

Biggest by capacity and size: Rungrado 1st of May Stadium, Pyongyang, North Korea

Claiming the title for largest in both size and capacity is North Korea's Rungrado 1st of May Stadium, which is distinguished by its unique roof composed of 16 sweeping, concrete arches.

Encompassing 207,000 square metres, the multi-purpose stadium boasts a capacity of 150,000 across eight levels and contains a 22,500-square-metre main arena alongside tracks, training halls and indoor pools.

Most expensive: SoFi Stadium, Los Angeles, California, US

Completed in 2020 at a cost of $5.5 billion, the SoFi Stadium in the Inglewood area of Los Angeles is the most expensive stadium ever built.

Its expansive structure, which holds 70,000 seats beneath a large curved roof, was designed by architecture studio HKS for development company Kroenke Sports & Entertainment to embody "the spirit of southern California".

Tallest: Montreal Olympic Stadium, Montreal, Canada 

A 165-metre-tall office tower beside the Montreal Olympic Stadium in Canada renders the concrete sports venue the tallest stadium in the world.

Originally realised by French architect Roger Taillibert for Montreal's 1976 summer Olympics, the stadium and its adjoining tower remain in use, with its retractable roof and interiors currently being revamped.

Largest free-spanning dome: The Singapore National Stadium, Singapore 

Engineering firm Arup led the design for the world's largest free-spanning dome, which shelters the multipurpose Singapore National Stadium.

Spanning 310 metres, the dome crowns the 55,000-seat multipurpose venue and features a retractable roof complete with an integrated lighting system.

Most sustainable: Climate Pledge Arena, Seattle, US

Completed in 2022, The Climate Pledge Arena became the first arena in the world to achieve Zero Carbon certification by the International Living Future Institute (ILFI).

Its structure was originally built for the 1962 World's Fair before being revamped by architecture studio Populous in line with sustainability initiatives set out by tech giant Amazon's Climate Pledge.

Longest spanning roof: Wembley Stadium, London, UK 

Designed by British studio Foster + Partners, London's Wembley Stadium is the largest stadium in the UK and features the longest single span roof support structure in the world.

The distinctive Wembley Arch has a steel lattice structure that stretches 315 metres over the 90,000-seat stadium, eliminating the need for any pillars to support the weight of its retractable roof.

Longest occupied: Deepdale, Preston, England 

Somewhat contentiously holding the spot as the longest-occupied stadium is the Deepdale stadium in England, which is home to Preston North End football team.

Built in 1875, the stadium has been in continuous use since 1878, with gradual additions over the years expanding its capacity to 23,000.

Highest altitude: Daniel Alcides Carrión Stadium, Cerro de Pasco, Peru 

Perched 4,338 metres above sea level in the city of Cerro de Pasco, the Estadio Daniel Alcides Carrión is recognised by global football association FIFA as the highest stadium in the world.

The open-air venue holds up to 12,000 people and serves as the home ground for Peruvian football teams Unión Minas and Ecosem Pasco.

item.content:encoded:
British youth organisation Girlguiding has unveiled the first update to its formerly regimented uniform in 30 years, intended to allow more freedom of expression.

Completed in collaboration with London studio Hemingway Design, the redesign includes 30 garments and 15 accessories and neckerchiefs created for Girlguilding's four age groups known as Rainbows, Brownies, Guides and Rangers.

Hemingway Design consulted 55,000 girls and women part of the groups, who co-designed the new uniform alongside the studio.

Although the range includes various garments, the emphasis is on a series of colourful tops that Girlguiding members can wear with any other items of their own clothing and still be considered in full uniform, from T-shirts to long-sleeves or hoodies.

The move comes in stark contrast with Girlguiding's previous, more formal uniforms, which were last updated in 1990 by British fashion designer Jeff Banks.

Research from Girlguiding found that 93 per cent of members, aged six to 16 years old, feel most comfortable when they can choose how to dress themselves. Forty-seven per cent of these girls agreed that they are at their most confident when they do so, too.

"Girlguiding's new uniform has been designed to be styled any way the girls want," said the youth organisation. "With a focus on self-expression and flexibility, to be considered in uniform, all members need to wear is a top from the new range."

The collection is characterised by a series of design features specifically requested by young members, from secret pockets in the waistbands of leggings and shorts to badge sashes that double as useful cross-body bags.

Read:

Christopher Raeburn designs new uniforms for V&A staff

Each of the age group's garments and accessories were designed with colour schemes that represent their histories.

For example, the Brownies' uniform was created in the group's recognisable brown and yellow hues.

The new Girlguiding uniform is being launched shortly before 6 September, when transgender girls and women will be forced to leave the youth organisation after the 2025 UK Supreme Court ruling on biological sex.

Hemingway Design previously created the 100th anniversary logo for the Dreamland amusement park in Margate, Kent. The studio also collaborated with local designer James Shaw to transform the Shepherd's Bush store interior for London charity shop, Traid.

The photography is courtesy of Girlguiding.

Dezeen Showroom: Australian design brand Soktas has released a sculptural wall lamp with a fluid glass shade mounted onto a metal plate.

Flo is intended for use in bedrooms, bathrooms and living areas, where it casts a gentle glow that pools on the wall around it.

According to Soktas, each fixture is individually made, resulting in subtle yet characterful variations that make each one unique, particularly the hand-blown glass shades.

The contrast between the metal disc that serves as the mounting plate and the more natural aesthetic of the glass results in a sculptural effect.

The glass element comes in various amorphous shapes. Users are able to select between warm white or warm bulb colours, and from a choice of metallic finishes for the plate.

The brand envisages them being installed solo or in pairs for a symmetrical appearance.

item.content:encoded:
Plans have been announced for a technology and innovation museum in Bengaluru, India, which has been designed by a consortium of international architecture studios.

Designed by Dublin-based Heneghan Peng Architects, London-based DROO and local studio Cadence Architects, the Museum of Innovation, Startup & Technology will house an innovation hub and exhibition hall within an overhauled factory at the city's historic NGEF campus.

Renders of the proposal reveal the factory's spacious, steel-framed volume complete with sawtooth roofs and large operable windows that will overlook a surrounding 105-acre forest.

According to the team, once complete, the Museum of Innovation, Startup & Technology, or MIST, will be the country's first museum dedicated exclusively to "modern India's journey in innovation, technology, and entrepreneurship".

"MIST is the public space Bengaluru has always needed – a place where the city can gather, connect, and create," Cadence Architects said.

"By transforming industrial heritage into a vibrant civic landscape, MIST fosters chance encounters, shared experiences, and collective exchange that fuel innovation, laying the foundation for Bengaluru's technological future."

Read:

Grand Egyptian Museum reaches completion in Giza

The building will encompass two institutions: the museum, which will contain exhibition space, and a government-led innovation hub dubbed the Innoverse. Its programmes will be split between two wings, which were conceptualised by the team as a "reciprocal structure" designed to facilitate cross-pollination.

"Rather than separating exhibition from production, the design creates an active exchange between the two institutions," the team said.

"This reciprocal structure transforms the two wings into an evolving ecosystem: MIST becomes a living archive of ongoing innovation, while Innoverse becomes a responsive workshop shaped by public curiosity and critique," it added.

Renders of the spaces reveal a lofty exhibition hall and a split-level communal area fitted out with large concrete columns and raised wooden platforms.

The Museum of Innovation, Startup & Technology forms part of a larger redevelopment of the existing NGEF campus into a cultural hub and "tree park", which is being developed by the local Karnataka Government.

Previous civic projects by Heneghan Peng Architects include the Grand Egyptian Museum, which reached completion in Giza last year, more than three decades after plans were announced.

Elsewhere, the sinuous Shenzhen Natural History Museum in China was recently completed by architecture studios 3XN, B+H Architects and Zhubo Design to "emulate a piece of landscape".

The renders are courtesy of DROO.

item.content:encoded:
Brunel University graduate Wing-See Yau has designed Yomi, a device that encourages children to read by linking their progress to the growth of digital pets.

Yomi is a compact device that converts reading time into points. These rewards are visualised in the form of a digital avatar that grows and evolves over the course of a 14-day cycle.

Yau developed the project during her final year of studies at Brunel University and presented it at the recent New Designers graduate fair, where it earned her the Cadbury-Mondelez International Award.

She told Dezeen that the self-initiated brief was informed by her childhood struggles with reading and her desire to make the experience more enjoyable for other children.

Her research identified that reading rates in the UK are declining, with only 33 per cent of children saying they enjoy reading and many turning instead to digital forms of entertainment.

With educators and parents increasingly keen to encourage young people to re-engage with reading from an early age, Yau set out to create a simple and fun solution that gamifies this activity.

"This approach showed me that daily streaks, visual feedback, badges and collectable items can significantly increase motivation and engagement," the designer told Dezeen.

"I wanted to incorporate these elements into my design to make reading feel more rewarding, interactive and enjoyable for students."

Yomi's name is derived from the Japanese word 'yomu' which means 'to read'. Yau explained that she wanted a short and simple name that represents the toy's playful and approachable nature.

The product aims to build positive associations by linking reading with a digital reward, transforming it into a fun and engaging activity.

Yau chose to develop a dedicated device, rather than an app, to prevent children from switching their attention to other activities like social media or games.

Daily reading time is converted into points that translate into the growth of a digital pet, from a baby to a child, teen, adult and culminating in a wise, mythic version of itself.

This form of incentive was informed by Yau's conversations with parents, who explained that children enjoy collecting and trading digital pets in video games. The idea of ownership, collection and social motivation also references the 1990s Tamagotchi toys.

Children use a built-in camera on the device to scan a book's barcode and begin a reading session. This also allows them to log the book's genre, with the most-read genre determining the bi-weekly outfit of their pet monkey.

Read:

Sweekar is world's "first emotionally intelligent" pocket-sized pet

They can choose to read aloud to their pet to practice their storytelling and pronunciation, or they can read silently to help build their focus and develop independent reading skills.

A built-in microphone recognises when the child is reading aloud. At the end of the session, the reading duration is converted into points that help the monkey to grow.

Reading cycles last for 14 days, at the end of which a new pet is introduced and the process begins again.

Long-term reading progress is mapped by the growth of the 'Tree of Knowledge' on a dedicated screen. Users can also collect a series of badges linked to the different genres of books they read.

Yau said she designed the product to support young children as they begin their reading journey, while also encouraging them to develop important life skills.

"Many children lack confidence when reading aloud in class, something I personally experienced," she added. "I wanted to address this issue in my product because it is key to supporting both literacy development and self-expression."

Other projects featured at New Designers this year included a service for formulating bespoke natural skincare products and a children's chair that transforms into an abstract interpretation of a castle.

The photography is courtesy of Wing-See Yau.

item.content:encoded:
Promotion: British furniture maker Joint Design Direction has used Autodesk's Fusion software to help expand its offering of homegrown workplace furniture, including a sleep pod that hides a full-size single bed.

The company now offers more than 30 products, which customers can personalise at will, all designed and manufactured at its headquarters in Dudley.

To support this level of complexity, Joint Design Direction (JDD) recently transitioned its team from standard computer-aided design (CAD) software to Autodesk Fusion.

Autodesk Fusion is a centralised, cloud-based platform that allows the company's 90-strong team to take products from concept to production in one place. It combines 3D modelling and simulation tools with computer-aided manufacturing (CAM) software for producing CNC machined parts.

The system also includes parametric design functionality, allowing JDD's production designers to tailor the final product to the needs of their clients – tweaking the height or width without having to redraw the whole design.

"Something that might have taken maybe three hours in AutoCAD takes three minutes now with Fusion," explained JDD production designer George Hopkins.

This has proved particularly helpful with the design of JDD's Yume Rest Pod, which incorporates a full-size single bed alongside a built-in table, multiple power outlets and adjustable lighting.

"For the design of our new rest pod, Fusion was particularly helpful," remembered production designer Charlie Adlem.

"During prototyping, we might need to adjust the design to make something wider to fit or determine the standardisation of the mattress," he added. "Parametric modelling came in handy. It's a click of a button rather than redrawing the whole thing."

The system also offers a more user-friendly interface than other options on the market, according to Adlem.

"I've used other software in the past, like SolidWorks and Rhino, and they seem so complicated compared to Fusion," he explained. "The user interface and icons are easy to use. The tools in Fusion are easy to pick up, and there are loads of tutorials online."

JDD didn't originally launch as an office furniture brand. The idea was born at London's 100% Design trade show in 2010, where founders James Mercy and Joe Duffell encountered the architects furnishing Google's headquarters in Europe, West Asia, and Africa.

They were having trouble sourcing specific products such as high-back sofas for the offices, and asked the JDD duo if they could help.

Fresh off their respective design degrees, the recently reunited school friends said yes despite having no prior experience in manufacturing. They told themselves, "we'd figure it out later", Mercy remembered.

Since then, the company has grown into a team of nearly 100, with showrooms in Birmingham, London, Glasgow and Dubai.

To bring furniture to life more quickly and efficiently, keep up with new demand and further grow the business, JDD decided to switch to Autodesk Fusion around a year ago,

The software, which combines design, data management and collaboration tools, has allowed members of the product design, manufacturing and production design teams to work from the same files for the first time.

Previously, product designer Henry Watson would model new JDD products in 3ds Max and test them in OnShape.

But to share his vision with the production design team, he would have to use stripped-back STEP files or 2D drawings.

"It really made sense for me to move into the same software with Fusion because now we can just share the documents and models," Watson said.

"When you share a STEP file, you lose all the history, notes, and little nuances because you're just exporting it as a dumb file. Then Charlie and George would have to rework it, and there was a lot of unnecessary back-and-forth communication. Now everything is there in one place."

The production designers, in turn, can then share the link for the final file with the team on the factory floor.

"Before we'd have to do drawings for the wood mill and the person assembling it," Hopkins remembered. "But now we share the file link, and they can just open it up on a tablet or a phone. It makes the process much faster."

Ultimately, JDD's founders said this improved workflow has proven beneficial not just for the team but also for the company as a whole.

"As long as things make their jobs easier or more efficient and enjoyable, then that's a win for me," Mercy said. "If using Fusion helps them, it helps the company."

item.content:encoded:
The first phase of a floating pool planned for the East River is nearing completion in Brooklyn, with a barge and an infiltration system designed to clean river water as it flows into the structure.

The in-progress pool, called Pool 1, is a rectangular pilot version of the larger +Pool concept, a cross-shaped floating pool that was first proposed for New York City in 2011 and has since faced a long road of city and state approvals.

Upon completion, Pool 1 is approved to float in the East River off of Pier 35 between the city's Two Bridges and Lower East Side neighbourhoods. A team is currently building the structure in Erie Basin Bargeport in Red Hook, Brooklyn before its installation at the Manhattan site.

The initial construction phases have focused on testing the concept's patented infiltration system and included towing the initial metal frame from Mississippi to New York City last summer.

The finalised version of +Pool is set to be a 9,000-square-foot (836 square metre) cross-shaped structure, where each arm holds different programming. Its filtration system, engineered in collaboration with Arup, is designed to filter river water into the pool's body without the use of chlorine.

The team's most recent update stated that "construction of the pilot pool's floating barge and innovative filtration system is nearing completion".

The team has also been prepping the site at Pier 35, including installing utility lines to power the pilot pool, and the eventual Olympic-length full design. The site initially "lacked the power, water, and sewer lines needed to operate the river-water-filtering swimming pool".

The project, run by non-profit Friends of + POOL, has grown from a local project into a statewide initiative.

It is supported by New York state governor Kathy Hochul under the NY Swims initiative launched in 2024. If the project is successful, +Pools would be deployed across water bodies in Upstate New York.

The +Pool team says it "has been actively coordinating with government partners" during the testing phase of the project and that a required "17 approvals across city, state, and federal agencies" have now been received.

The team said it is also coordinating with the Brooklyn Bridge-Montgomery Coastal Resilience (BMCR), a coastal flood-prevention project that shares the Pier 35 site.

Read:

Central Park recreation facility designed as "ultimate fusion of landscape and architecture"

A public demonstration of the project has been pushed back until 2027 from its original date this year, as +Pool is unable to "attach to the permitted sewer lines for waste discharge until the critical waterfront shoreline resiliency project is complete".

"While this shift comes at a cost to the organisation and the project, those realities will feel insignificant when we are living in a New York City that has advanced infrastructure to protect from storm surges while opening up safe public river access for healthful recreation," said Friends of + POOL managing director Kara Meyer.

The founders of architecture studio Playlab Inc Archie Lee Coates IV and Jeff Franklin, architect and founder of Food Architects, Dong-Ping Wong and architect Oana Stănescu first developed the project as a group of young designers before it went fully public.

Coates IV, Franklin and Stănescu are still attached to the project, but Wong has claimed he was frozen out of the project after raising concerns about diversity to the board.

Elsewhere in New York, a public pool in Central Park recently received a restoration.

The photography is courtesy Friends of + POOL.
